title: The Promise of Low Energy Ion Scattering for Probing the Outermost Atomic Layers of Materials. An Important Method That is Complementary to X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy.
content: X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) is the most widely used and powerful tool for chemically analyzing surfaces. It is sensitive to all the elements except hydrogen and helium, and it provides both elemental and chemical state information about surfaces. Conventional XPS with Al K alpha X-rays probes up to 10 nm into materials, and angle-resolved (AR)-XPS increases the surface sensitivity of the technique. However, it is often important to probe both more and less deeply into materials. The first of these problems is addressed by hard XPS (HAXPES), which uses (more) energetic X-rays to increase the analysis depth of the technique down to ca. 20 nm. The second of these issues is more challenging. Even with AR-XPS, it is often not entirely clear which elements are at the outermost surface of a material. However, an understanding of the outermost atomic layer of materials can be crucial in various technologies. For example, it is not possible to thoroughly understand an atomic layer deposition (ALD) process unless the outermost atomic layers in the deposition steps are elucidated. In addition, heterogeneous catalysts usually operate at their outermost atomic layers. Accordingly, we have increasingly combined XPS and low energy ion scattering (LEIS), where this latter method is sensitive to the outermost atomic layers of materials. In this talk, I introduce LEIS, describe its capabilities, and then discuss the multi-instrument characterization of materials with XPS, LEIS, and other techniques. Time permitting, I also discuss various data science/informatics tools we have used for the analysis of this data.
